name: The single primal substance (arche)
plain_explanation: Each Milesian philosopher asked what one basic 'stuff' everything else is made of and can be transformed back into: Thales said water, Anaximander said an indefinite 'boundless' substance, and Anaximenes said air.
precise_definition: The idea, foundational to the Milesian school, that the apparent diversity of the world's substances is reducible to transformations of a single underlying material principle.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats the very asking of this question -- rather than the specific (and mostly wrong) answers -- as marking the beginning of philosophy and science together, since it is a general, naturalistic hypothesis open in principle to reasoning and evidence rather than myth.
historical_origin: First proposed by Thales (water) in early sixth-century B.C. Miletus, then revised successively by Anaximander and Anaximenes.
examples: Thales: water as the original substance, with the earth resting on water
Anaximander: the 'boundless' (apeiron), infinite and ageless, encompassing all worlds
Anaximenes: air, which becomes fire when rarefied and water, then earth, then stone when condensed
objections: Anaximander's own argument that water (or any single known element) could not be primal, since it would have already conquered and eliminated the opposing elements
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anaximenes' theory of condensation and rarefaction, making differences between substances purely quantitative, influenced Pythagoras and much later speculation.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Thales' remark that 'all things are full of gods' shows the doctrine was not fully separated from religious ways of speaking, even while moving toward naturalistic explanation.
